description: An extent that is not finite is **no extent at all**. Upstream's `Extent.js` ends `if (!Number.isFinite(min) || !Number.isFinite(max)) { warn; min = max = undefined; }`, and the infinity is never filtered on the way in — `Number.isFinite` is asked of the *result*, so one infinite value takes the whole extent with it. The domain is then `[undefined, undefined]`, the scale answers `NaN` for everything and its axis draws no ticks and no labels. Four columns say which part of that rule is doing the work: `word` holds the text `Infinity`, which `Number` reads as a number; `calc` reaches an infinity by dividing by zero, so the rule is not about strings; `words` holds no number anywhere, where the extent stays at its `[+Infinity, -Infinity]` start and is discarded for the same reason; and `ok` is ordinary, so the fixture says what this costs and what it does not. The first axis is the observable one: with a finite domain it draws labels, and with no extent it draws nothing. The `extent` **transform** publishes the same rule into a signal, and it is written out here too — the two used to be separate transcriptions and only one of them was right.

text.signal: 'word ' + scale('word', datum.ok) + ' calc ' + scale('calc', datum.ok) + ' words ' + scale('words', datum.ok) + ' ok ' + scale('ok', datum.ok)
'extent of word: [' + wordExtent + '] extent of ok: [' + okExtent + ']'
